## Setting Up the Problem

This is a classic base-rate fallacy problem. Using Bayes' theorem:

- P(Disease) = 1/500 = 0.002
- P(No Disease) = 0.998
- P(Test+ | Disease) = 0.98 (sensitivity)
- P(Test+ | No Disease) = 1 − 0.95 = 0.05 (false positive rate)

**Total probability of testing positive:**

P(Test+) = P(Disease)·P(Test+|Disease) + P(No Disease)·P(Test+|No Disease)
P(Test+) = (0.002 × 0.98) + (0.998 × 0.05)
P(Test+) = 0.00196 + 0.04990
P(Test+) = 0.05186

**Applying Bayes' theorem:**

P(Disease | Test+) = 0.00196 / 0.05186 ≈ 0.0377941...

Converting to a percentage: **3.7794...%** → rounds to **3.78%**

## Why This Is Counterintuitive

Even with a 98% sensitive, 95% specific test, a positive result only means a ~3.78% chance of actually having the condition. This is because the disease is rare (0.2% prevalence), so the pool of healthy people is huge (998 out of 1000) — and even a small 5% false-positive rate among that huge healthy pool generates far more false positives (≈49.9 per 1000) than true positives (≈1.96 per 1000). Most positive results come from healthy people who were false-flagged, not from people who actually have the condition.

FINAL ANSWER: 3.78
